Effect of Earthworms on Achillea millefolium 
(Common Yarrow) Plant Growth 
 
Sofia Gomez Almazan, Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney 
 
Team: D.A.V. E. Team Number: 21295 
 
Skyview High School, Vancouver, WA 
 
Plant The Moon Challenge, Spring 2025, High School Division

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 2 
Introduction 
​
To establish colonies on The Moon or Mars, astronauts need a sustainable way to 
survive by growing various plants for sustenance and medicinal purposes. In the “Plant the 
Moon Competition”, the researchers realized that there was a very strong focus made by other 
teams on planting food on The Moon or Mars and that there was a lack of medicinal plants 
being researched. The researchers believed that Achillea millefolium (Common yarrow) is a 
hardy, useful tool for astronauts to use on the Moon, due to the yarrow's healing properties it 
can be useful for allowing astronauts to “grow their First Aid kit”. 
The researchers believed that further exploration into medicinal plants could be an 
extremely valuable asset in the health of astronauts. Plants like yarrow can be used to treat 
wounds, colds, and other common ailments. However, the task of growing plants on the Moon 
or Mars has proven itself to be difficult. Lunar soil has many different types of minerals, but its 
carbon and nitrogen levels- two important nutrients- are dependent upon solar winds, meaning 
that the levels can, and do fluctuate (Gibson 58-59). This could mean that the lunar soil has 
insufficient amounts of nitrogen at different times of the year or even day by day. Also, lunar 
soil has very poor water retention, meaning the plant that the researchers chose needs to be 
drought tolerant if they were to choose lunar soil. On the other hand, Martian soil is water 
retaining, so the researchers would have to choose a plant that needs more water for it to 
survive in Martian regolith. Also, the amount of nitrogen in Martian soil has been shown to 
decrease, which is not good for the environment of plants (Mancinelli abstract). In contrast, the 
Miracle-Gro Potting Soil that was used during this project contains nitrogen: 0.21%, phosphate: 
0.11% potash: 0.16%, and other nutrients (HEB). While this does supplement the 
aforementioned lack of nitrogen, researchers suspect that this may not be enough to grow the 
plants by itself due to the fact that potting soil is sometimes combined with Earth soil. Studies 
have shown that the main nutrients that plants need are nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, 
magnesium, calcium, sulfur, boron, iron, copper, manganese, chlorine, molybdenum, and zinc 
(Uchida 31-32, 49-51). Since nitrogen is such a large factor, the researchers decided to 
primarily focus on the decomposition/ nitrogen cycle. By using earthworms, the researchers 
believed that the worms will go through the same processes that they go through on Earth, that 
is adding nutrients/nitrogen to the soil through their ability to decompose the nutrients already 
present in the potting soil/regolith. The researchers chose lunar soil and yarrow seeds due to

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 3 
their medicinal properties. The researchers also believed that the amount of nutrients in the 
potting soil would be sufficient to sustain the worms and give the plants their necessary 
nutrients due to the yarrow’s ability to live in non-ideal conditions. 
 
Experimental Design 
 
(Figure 1. Initial Grow Setup, (Figure 2. Initial Grow Setup, (Figure 3. Initial Grow Setup, 
zoomed out) zoomed in) plant close up) 
 
In the Skyview High School building, the researchers set up their experiment on a grow 
light rack in a temperature-controlled room. The researchers adjusted the height of the rack so 
that all plants were an equal distance from the grow light. If they were to grow too tall, the 
height of the grow light could be readjusted to make sure the plants didn’t exceed the limit for 
distance to the growth lights. The overhead lights were only ever turned on for brief periods of 
time for recording videos, and the nearby window always had the blinds shut. The researchers 
would take out the plants from the setup for brief measurements and observations, giving all of 
the plants approximately five minutes out of the setup. The researchers determined that the 
small amount of time out of the system and the introduced light from the overhead lights was 
negligible due to the ratio of time in the controlled system to the time outside of it. The 
researchers mixed the soil-worm mixture for each pot. The researchers planted the yarrow with 
the provided N-95 mask as a safety precaution to prevent the ingestion of the lunar soil through 
breathing. The researchers found that each worm weighed approximately 1g. The reason why

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 4 
the researchers made these experimental design choices was to control as many outside 
variables as possible, while still keeping it simplistic. The researchers have complete control 
over the lighting, the water, and the amount of soil/ worms. This makes the experiment as a 
whole more accurate. 
The researchers decided to use lunar soil for this experiment due to the choice of plant. 
The researchers wanted to use a medicinal plant, and in their research, found yarrow. Yarrow is 
drought-tolerant, meaning that it survives well in dry environments. Yarrow won’t survive as 
well in moist environments, as the plant needs well-drained soil and thrives in areas with less 
than 1 inch of precipitation per week (COMMON 3). Since Martian soil is water-retaining, the 
researchers thought it was the obvious solution to pick the lunar soil. 
There are a variety of reasons why the researchers decided to use yarrow. First of all, 
the plant is extremely hardy. It is known to be invasive in other countries, spreading very 
quickly due to its resilience. Yarrow is well known for being drought tolerant, which is perfect 
for lunar soil’s low water retention. The main reason why yarrow would be a valuable tool for 
astronauts is its medicinal properties. This plant has been used in traditional medicine for 
Native American tribes and in Greece for thousands of years. Just by rubbing yarrow on your 
skin or brewing it to make yarrow tea, it can be used to treat earaches, coughing, toothaches, 
head colds, throat irritation, nausea, and fevers. It is also known for being used as a laxative, a 
way to normalize the menstrual cycle, a pain killer, and it can stop bleeding (COMMON 3-4). 
Yarrow can also be used as a vitamin/ mineral supplement for astronauts since it contains 
vitamins A and C and the minerals potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, calcium, zinc, 
phosphorus, and niacin (Produce). However, there are potential drawbacks associated with 
yarrow. Yarrow can cause allergic reactions like skin rashes. It is also known to possibly induce 
menstruation, and cause miscarriages. (Apothecary, Sinai) The researchers decided that 
although these possible side effects exist, the plant could still be useful for astronauts, as long 
as pregnant women don’t use it. There are still many ways the plant can be used for good. 
Having medicinal plants as a method of First Aid allows spacecraft to have more room in their 
cargo for other supplies instead of just medicine. Also, replanting effectively gives astronauts 
the ability to have as much yarrow as they need. The researchers hope that this experiment 
could be used to inspire other research on other medicinal plants, as they believe that these 
plants are valuable to the safety of astronauts on the Moon or Mars.

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 5 
The reason why researchers decided to use worms to make the yarrow grow taller is 
because worms affect the Earth’s environment. Worms play a critical role not only in the 
nitrogen cycle but in providing nutrients to the soil (Blanchart, 1999). The researchers believe 
that the worms will have an overall positive effect on the plants by providing nitrogen and 
nutrients to the soil. 
 
Variables 
For our independent variable, researchers changed the amount of worms per pot. For the 
dependent variable, researchers measured the height of the tallest leaf of each plant in 
centimeters. The variables that the researchers controlled were the soil pH, the amount of light, 
the pot size, the amount of seeds, and the time to grow. 
 
Hypothesis 
​
If the researchers were to put different amounts of worms into different plant pots with 
lunar soil, potting soil, and yarrow seeds, then the plant with more worms would grow taller 
because, on Earth, worms help supply nutrients to plants in Earth soil, so the worms should 
have the same effect with the lunar regolith. 
 
Materials 
1.​ 5, Medium-sized plant pots 
2.​ 500g of lunar soil 
3.​ 482g of potting soil (Miracle Gro) 
4.​ 18g of worms 
5.​ Water 
6.​ Grow Light 
7.​ N-95 Masks 
8.​ Popsicle sticks 
9.​ Sharpie 
10.​Ruler 
11.​Scale

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 6 
Procedure 
1.​ Using an N-95 mask as a precaution, use a scale to weigh 100g of lunar soil and 
add the soil into each plant pot. 
2.​ In the first two pots, weigh out and add 100g of potting soil. 
3.​ For the 1% pot, weigh out and add 98g of lunar soil and 2g of worms. (Approx. 
2 worms) 
4.​ For the 3% pot, weigh out and add 94g of lunar soil and 6g of worms. 
(Approx. 6 worms) 
5.​ For the 5% pot, weigh out and add 90g of lunar soil and 10g of worms. 
(Approx. 10 worms) 
6.​ Mark each pot accordingly with the popsicle sticks and Sharpie 
7.​ Add an equal amount of seeds per pot, and push them down with your thumb 
very lightly into the soil so that they go to a depth of about 1/8th of an inch. 
8.​ Set up a grow light, making sure that it is level so that each plant pot gets an 
equal amount of light. 
9.​ Carefully set each plant underneath the grow light 
10.​Water each plant as much as is needed for the soil to be moist 
11.​Measure the height of the tallest part of the yarrow once a week 
 
Data 
Data was first measured on 2/26. During the first week of the growth period, researchers 
planted the seeds. In one of the weeks, there was a snow storm which shut down the 
researcher’s school, which prevented them from checking on the plants. During the second 
week the plants continued sprouting. The researchers decided to take data after the plants had 
grown higher in an effort to avoid damage.

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 7 
 
Figure 4. Table of Days Of Data Collection and Height (cm) 
 
Figure 5. Growth Of Plants Overtime 
 
Observations (2/26): All of the plants except for 3% started growing in a more bush-like way, 
some pots (like 1%) are more clumped together while others (like 5%) are spread out more, the 
most "lively" looking plants are 1% and 5%. 
Observations (3/5): There is one clump of mold in the 1% plant pot. The leaves in all of the 
pots except for the 3% are all beginning to look more like a yarrow bush (the leaves are 
separating, it’s looking greener, etc.) 
Observations (3/12): The back 0% was very dehydrated in contrast to the rest of the plants. 5% 
and 1% are in the lead for height. 5% has a couple of very tall leaves. 1% is more full of tall 
leaves. The dehydrated 0% looks the palest underneath the light and the 1% looks the greenest. 
Observations (3/19): The plants are very green! Underneath the light, they look pale, but 
outside of it, they are all a deep green. The fullest plant pot is 1%, and the tallest plant pot is 
5%, however, it doesn’t look as healthy as the other plants. In how healthy they look, the order

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 8 
would be: 1%, back 0%, front 0%, 5%, and 3%. There are new sprouts in the 5% and both of 
the 0 %s. The 5% is more spindly than the 1%. 
Observations (3/26): Both 0%s are very green. When watering the 5%, you can hear the worms 
moving around. 5% is becoming more yellow, in future experiments it might need more water. 
1% is very green and has started sprouting even more. 
Observations (Unearthing): The front 0% had dry-ish soil and lots of root growth. The 0% 
back’s leaves were tangled together, it was the most withered due to lack of water, and it had 
lots of roots. Researchers were unable to find any worms in the 1% plant lot. Most of the roots 
of this plant were at the bottom and so was the lunar soil. The roots were weak/ easy to take 
apart, and they formed the most around areas with clumped lunar soil. 
3% had 5/6 of the worms still living. Also, the worms were longer and wider. 
5%: Every worm survived in this plant pot (10/10) and grew. This plant pot also had the least 
compacted soil. All of the plant pots except 3% had their roots pushed out to the edges. 
 
Analysis & Results 
​
On the last day of the experiment, the 1% plant pot and the 5% plant pot were tied for 
the tallest height at 16 cm. For all of the days leading up to the last however, the 5% plant pot 
was overall the tallest plant. The researchers believe this is due to the amount of worms that 
were added to this pot. Each plant pot had a unique way they grew. 
First of all, the controls (both of the 0% plant pots) behaved the same, up until day 3/12. 
On this day, the back plant pot was found to be more dehydrated than the other. Also, the tallest 
leaf of this pot was 0.5 cm shorter than the other. However, the next week, this pot grew to be 
taller than the front 0% pot for the rest of the experiment, as shown in Figures 4 and 5. This is 
strange behavior given the fact that these two plants were given the same conditions. These 
differences are likely due to a variable that the researchers couldn’t control. If the potting soil 
wasn’t mixed very well in manufacturing, then one of the plants may have had higher nutrient 
density than the other. If this is the case, then the potting soil nutrient density could have 
affected the other plant pots for the rest of the experiment. 
For the 1% plant pot, it overall was the healthiest of all of the pots, even if it wasn’t as 
tall as the 5% for most of the experiment. Upon unearthing the plant, we found no worms 
within the soil. Also, the mold clump that the researchers discovered on 3/5 was suspected to be

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 9 
a clump of lunar soil. The researchers were confused about how this plant could have thrived in 
the way it did without the worms and came to the conclusion that the worms died, and then 
decomposed, releasing nutrients into the soil in that way instead of how lying worms release 
nutrients. This plant shows another positive of using worms, which is that if they do not 
survive, their dead waste material can still help the plant after their death. Even though this is 
the case, further amendments to the experiment are recommended for long-term plant growth. 
For the 3% plant pot, given the metrics between 1% and 5% in Figure 4, researchers 
believed that the growth would have been in between the two of those pots. However, this pot 
didn’t sprout at all. The researchers have a couple of theories for why the plant pot with 3% 
worms had no growth. Firstly, the researchers believe that the worms may have been fatigued 
from being in the bin/ bait shop for too long. Secondly, the soil, being poor at retaining water, 
could have made them dry out. Third, and the most likely of the three, the worms could have 
eaten the yarrow seeds from hunger. Upon unearthing the plants, the researchers found that 5 
out of the 6 worms in the pot survived, meaning that one of the worms likely died from one of 
the two causes above. The reason why this plant didn’t show any mold even with one of the 
worms dying could be explained by the fact that the other 5 worms were still alive. The 
researchers believe that the worms ate the yarrow seeds, and then proceeded to eat the body of 
the dead worm (due to the fact the researchers did not find the dead worm’s body) which gave 
them enough nutrients from the soil and from the seeds/ dead worm to sustain themselves over 
the grow period. The soil would likely have provided enough nutrients to the worms like with 
the 5% pot, however, they instead went for the seeds/ body. 
For the 5% plant pot, over the grow period this plant was equal in height or taller than 
every other plant. However, in the researcher's observations, this plant was shown to be the 
least healthy other than with the 3% plant pot. Overall the leaves were more spindly, and paler, 
and the bush was the least full of the group. Upon unearthing, this plant had all 10 of the 10 
worms alive. This led researchers to believe that the cause of the plant’s height was the increase 
in nutrients supplied by the worms.

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 10 
Conclusion 
​
The data the researchers found did agree with the hypothesis that if the researchers were 
to put different amounts of worms into different plant pots with lunar soil, potting soil, and 
yarrow seeds, then the plant with more worms would grow taller because, on Earth, worms help 
supply nutrients to plants in Earth soil, so the worms should have the same effect with the lunar 
regolith. 
The 5% plant pot (the one with the most amount of worms) was tied with the 1% plant 
pot at the end of the experiment. Researchers believe that this was due to the nutrients supplied 
by the worms in both scenarios, with the living worms in 5% and the dead waste supplied by 
1%. Initially, researchers believed that the nutrients present in the potting soil would have been 
enough to sustain the worms through the growing period. While the nutrients in the soil did 
sustain the 5% pot, the 1% and 3% show that an amendment should be made to this 
experiment. Researchers believe that if this experiment were to be repeated, it would be 
recommended to use worm food within the mixture in order to prevent the deaths from the 1% 
plant pot and the death of the worms/ seeds in the 3% plant pot. Another change that 
researchers would make to this experiment would be the ability to find nitrogen levels in the 
soil. Adding this could confirm suspicions of the worms releasing more nitrogen into the soil 
through the nitrogen cycle. Also, finding a way to test the nutrients of the beginning soil instead 
of relying on the potting soil’s website could lead researchers in the future to have more control 
over the starting soil, leading to the controls behaving in the same way. The last change the 
researchers would make to the experiment is determining a method of differentiating mold and 
clumped lunar soil. We originally marked 1% as having spots of mold in it, but upon further 
examination, the researchers believe this may have been a false positive given the fact during 
the unearthing, they couldn’t find the mold. While this could have been mold given that the 
worms in the pot died, researchers believe it was more likely that the worms completely 
decomposed, providing the plant with nutrients, leading to its height and fullness. If a method 
was developed to differentiate the two materials, this experiment may have been more accurate 
to when the worms in the pots died. Overall, this experiment was successful in the growing of 
yarrow in lunar soil. Researchers believe that with further experiments, the effect of worms on 
medicinal plants, especially yarrow, can assist astronauts with their healing properties as long 
as the methods of sustaining the worms and plants are expanded upon.

Casey Flinn, Olivia Countney, Sofia Gomez Almazan, 11
